{"id": "2:286/q01", "question": "What limit does God place on obligation?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q01/p1", "position": "God requires only what a person can perform.", "reasons": "FARRA: وسعها is a noun meaning capacity; its vocalic pattern parallels the alternatives in وجد and جهد. MUSNAD-AHMAD reporting أبو هريرة: The report glosses the capacity verse as assigning the soul the good it earns and charging it with the evil it acquires. TUSTARI: A soul's “capacity” means its strength or ability. TAB-FULL: God burdens a soul only with what lies within its capacity, imposing no constriction or excessive hardship in religious duties. TAB-FULL: Al-Tabari distinguishes forgetfulness caused by neglect from forgetfulness caused by incapacity or weak memory. TAB-FULL reporting الضحاك: Al-Dahhak says it asks not to be burdened with deeds beyond their capacity. ZAJJAJ: God imposes no obligation, such as fasting, prayer, or charity, beyond a person's capacity. IBNABIHATIM reporting سفيان: Sufyān applies the capacity limit to spending: only what one can afford. IBNABIHATIM reporting سفيان الثوري: Sufyān al-Thawrī interprets the capacity limit as performance of obligatory duties. THALABI reporting بعضهم: One interpretation holds that God accounts for settled convictions and intentions, while passing thoughts without resolve are exempt under the capacity verse; the oath verse supplies a parallel. JISHUMI: Ṭāqa means strength or capacity. JISHUMI: God has not imposed commands and prohibitions beyond people’s capacity, removing their excuse. JISHUMI reporting أبو مسلم: Alternatively, it begins a new divine statement to the Messenger and believers, clarifying that earlier commands and prohibitions did not exceed capacity. BAGHAWI-FULL: The petition asks not to be charged with deeds beyond their capacity. TABRISI reporting سفيان بن عيينة: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna calls it a good interpretation that God does not impose a person's full limit of capacity, which would exhaust their effort. TABRISI: A third explanation treats this as devotional petition, though God does not impose on anyone a burden beyond their capacity. RAZI-FULL: If the believers speak the clause, it follows their “we hear and obey”: since God mercifully requires only what is within capacity, they must respond with obedience as servants. RAZI-FULL: Al-Rāzī ends this dispute by asking God to show mercy to their incapacity and limited understanding and forgive their errors, affirming that they seek only truth. RAZI-FULL reporting بعض الناس: Some accept a distinction: kasb can be for oneself or another, while iktisāb is only what one acquires for oneself; one can be a breadwinner for one's family but not an acquirer for them. RAZI-FULL reporting النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: Imran ibn Husayn reports that the Prophet instructed the ill to pray sitting, or on their side if unable; jurists read inability as severe hardship, not literal incapacity. No grading is stated. QURTUBI-FULL: This categorical statement says no bodily or inward act is imposed beyond a person’s capacity, understanding, and constitution, relieving the Muslims’ anxiety about thoughts. QURTUBI-FULL reporting أبو هريرة: Abu Hurayra’s quoted couplet says God burdens no soul beyond its capacity and a hand gives only what it has. BAYDAWI-FULL: God burdens a soul only with what its ability can contain, by grace and mercy; alternatively, He gives less than its utmost capacity, making the duty manageable and easy. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The apparent sense is a fresh divine report: God burdens people in inward and bodily acts only with what their capacity, faculties, and constitution can bear. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting قيل: An alternative makes these words part of the Messenger's and believers' speech: after saying “we hear and obey,” they reason that God asks only what they can bear. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting الضحاك: Al-Dahhak, with Ibn Zayd, interprets the prayer as asking not to be burdened with deeds beyond one's capacity. IBNKATHIR-FULL reporting جابر: Jabir reports that after this verse was revealed, Gabriel told the Prophet that God had praised him and his community and invited him to ask; the Prophet then asked for the closing supplication beginning, 'God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.' BURHAN: The author cites the verse's concise statement of capacity, responsibility, and earned reward as an example of eloquent concision. BIQAI-FULL: Ṭāqa means ability or capacity; the request asks not to be made to bear what they cannot manage. ALUSI-FULL: God's practice is to impose only what a person can bear, indeed sometimes less: five daily prayers despite capacity for more, and Ramadan despite capacity for additional fasting. ALUSI-FULL reporting قيل: An alternative makes both clauses part of believers' separate utterances, praising them for gratitude that duties fit their capacity and that good benefits them while evil harms them, not God; Al-Alusi calls this remote in one respect and close in another. ELMALILI: He reads the clause as showing the benefit of obligatory duties and urging believers to spend capacity beyond them on voluntary worship and good works, a recommendation called nadb. ELMALILI reporting الله: A qudsi hadith cited here says the believing servant continues drawing near to God through supererogatory acts, supporting the exhortation to spend surplus capacity in good works. ELMALILI: A second construal says properly directed effort earns benefit, while blind striving after harm costs the person; capacity-calibrated divine duties guide people toward benefit and away from loss. ELMALILI: A person who fails to learn religious and legal duties, or fails to review them after learning them, is not excused for later forgetting; some causes of forgetfulness are within human capacity to prevent. ELMALILI: “Pardon us” asks God to erase the effects of sins. People pledge sincere obedience but still fall short, cannot fully spend the God-given capacity and will in His path, and therefore ask through grace rather than earned merit; though deeds remain in divine knowledge, God can remove their consequences. ELMALILI: An obligation beyond given capacity would be torment rather than a duty; God appoints such torment as just punishment for refusing His law, as in the command to enter Hell at 40:76, with worldly examples among lawbreaking peoples and individuals. ELMALILI: The supplications that follow are connected to the wisdom that duties are proportionate to capacity and direct people away from harm. ELMALILI: God's obligations leave capacity beyond what is required, allowing rest and voluntary good deeds after duties; the five daily prayers do not exhaust a person's ability to act. ELMALILI: The same capacity principle governs how communal obligations fall on individuals, and the total duties assigned to one person must not exceed that person's capacity. ELMALILI: Elmalılı summarizes the greatest principle of legislative wisdom as duties being proportionate to the capacity of the person charged. IBNASHUR-FULL: The clause is circumstantial from nafs and explains capacity: good benefits the soul and evil harms it, marked respectively by li and ʿala. TABATABAI: Wasʿ means capacity; it first denotes spatial breadth, then metaphorically the capacity that contains a person’s possible acts. TABATABAI: Earning is evidence that a person acquires benefit or harm through acts that lie within their capacity."}, {"id": "2:286/q01/p2", "position": "God requires only what a person can perform, with ease in religion.", "reasons": "TAB-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn Abbas says the believers were given breadth in religion, citing the absence of hardship, God’s desire for ease, and the command to fear Him as able. IBNABIHATIM reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbās says God eased believers' religion, linking this to no hardship (22:78), willing ease (2:185), and fear as much as possible (64:16). IBNABIHATIM reporting محمد بن كعب القرظي: Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb says people were not charged with work they could not bear; others are reported to agree. IBNATIYYA-FULL: This accords with verses saying God intends ease, places no hardship in religion, and requires mindfulness as far as possible. QURTUBI-FULL reporting ابن خويزمنداد: Ibn Khuwayzimandad says the verse’s apparent sense can rebut claims that a religious duty is unduly burdensome, in line with no hardship in religion and the report that religion is easy. NASAFI-FULL reporting شرح التأويلات: Obligation is limited to acts a person can perform, since responsibility concerns deeds within one’s ability. IBNKATHIR-FULL reporting رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: A Prophetic report says he was sent with the upright, easy religion. DURR-FULL reporting ابن عباس: Ibn ʿAbbas says God eased religious duties for believers, linking this to no hardship in religion (22:78), God’s desire for ease (2:185), and fearing God as much as possible (64:16)."}, {"id": "2:286/q01/p3", "position": "Capacity here is manageable ability below a person's utmost exertion.", "reasons": "THALABI reporting ابن عباس: In another account, the verse concerns believers specifically: God eased religious duties and required only what they can do, as shown by verses affirming ease, no hardship, and duty according to capacity. QUSHAYRI: In perfect mercy, God sets people's charge at their capacity and far below that limit, out of gentleness and grace. WAHIDI-BASIT reporting ابن عباس: In another transmission, Ibn Abbas says God imposed only what believers can do, citing God's desire for ease, removal of hardship, and the command to fear Him as able. WAHIDI-BASIT: The best explanation is that capacity here is below full ability: God graciously burdens people with less than their maximum; Sufyan ibn Uyayna glosses it as ease, since a full-capacity burden would exhaust them. {"id": "2:286/q02", "question": "What does وُسْعَهَا mean?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q02/p1", "position": "God requires only what a person can perform.", "reasons": "IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB: Wusʿ means a person's capacity. {"id": "2:286/q05", "question": "Can God impose an impossible duty?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q05/p1", "position": "An impossible duty is rationally possible, and some argue it has occurred.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ: Imposing what is absolutely beyond capacity is impossible; if the phrase means burdensome, God may do as He wills. THALABI reporting الزجاج: Al-Zajjaj says burdening beyond ability is impossible if it means beyond one's capacity, but possible if it means what feels heavy; Israel's commanded self-killing was burdensome in the latter sense. IBNATIYYA-FULL: Those denying rational possibility of impossible duties read the verse as saying God neither does nor has imposed one; Ibn Atiyya says this is not explicit. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting أبو الحسن الأشعري وجماعة من المتكلمين: Al-Ashari and other theologians hold that imposing an impossible duty is rationally possible, not religiously forbidden, and signals certain punishment. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting فرقة: One group says impossible duty occurred in Abu Lahab's case: he was foretold as doomed to disbelief while commanded to believe. IBNATIYYA-FULL reporting الطبري والزجاج: Al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj deny impossible duties: forgetting means omitted duties, error intentional disobedience, and the burden Israelite obligations and punishments. RAZI-FULL reporting المعتزلة: Their second premise is that ability precedes the act; otherwise an unbeliever commanded to believe would not be able to do so, making the command impossible. RAZI-FULL reporting أصحابنا: Al-Rāzī's Ashʿarite colleagues say rational proofs establish that impossible commands do occur, so this verse must be interpreted. RAZI-FULL: The second argument says acts depend on motives created by God; if motives instead came from the person, an infinite regress follows, while a determining motive makes the alternative impossible, yet the unbeliever is commanded to believe. RAZI-FULL: The third argument says a command issued when motives are equal requires contradictory equality and preference; if one motive prevails, the preferred is necessary and the other impossible. RAZI-FULL: The fifth argument says people do not know the detailed count of movements and rests in an act such as moving a finger; since they did not intend that precise count, they do not create it, and an undetermined preference is impossible. RAZI-FULL: A second answer defines command as notice that action brings reward and omission brings punishment; where an act is impossible, the statement is not a real command but notice of punishment and one's creation for Hell. RAZI-FULL: Punishing a forgetful person is not rationally impossible: fear of later punishment can sustain memory, though constant vigilance is difficult, making a request for pardon fitting. QURTUBI-FULL reporting أبو الحسن الأشعري وجماعة من المتكلمين: Al-Ashari and a group of theologians hold that imposing the impossible is rationally possible, as a sign that the person will be punished, without compromising doctrine. QURTUBI-FULL: The scholars agree that impossible obligations do not occur in revealed law, and this verse signals their absence. QURTUBI-FULL reporting فرقة: One group says the impossible occurred in Abu Lahab’s case: he was commanded to accept a whole law that included the prediction he would never believe. QURTUBI-FULL reporting فرقة: Another group says impossible obligation never occurred; a consensus is reported on this position. BAYDAWI-FULL: The plea concerns tribulation and punishment, or duties beyond human capacity; its wording indicates that imposing an impossible duty is possible, since the prayer seeks escape from it. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: The verse resolves the believers' concern over thoughts in 2:284 and establishes that impossible demands are not legally imposed; he compares it with God's wish for ease in 2:185. ABUHAYYAN-FULL: Some infer from this verse that God may impose a duty beyond human capacity. BIQAI-FULL: The supplications proceed from lighter requests to heavier ones, teaching that God did not punish forgetfulness or error, impose burdens, demand the impossible, or withhold pardon and mercy. BURSEVI: This shows that God has not actually imposed an impossible burden, not that such imposition is intrinsically impossible: its occurrence would make God's statement false, while an unrestricted negation does not establish impossibility. ALUSI-FULL: On either gloss of wusʿ, the verse shows that impossible burdens do not actually occur, but it does not prove that such imposition is logically impossible. ALUSI-FULL reporting قيل: Another view makes the request broader than the preceding one: the burden is pictured as impossible to bear for emphasis. ALUSI-FULL reporting قيل: A further view treats this as asking to avoid literally impossible obligations and argues that the request proves such obligations are possible; Al-Alusi judges the argument weak. TABATABAI: God may prevent wrongdoing by blocking its means or requiring precaution; burdens imposed as punishment for a person's prior bad choice are not intrinsically impossible obligations. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Against theologians who deem an impossible divine burden permissible to protect unrestricted power and will, the author reads the verse as confirming that a wise God does not impose what exceeds capacity, in keeping with justice and a rational basis for accountability."}, {"id": "2:286/q05/p2", "position": "An intrinsically impossible duty cannot be imposed.", "reasons": "ZAJJAJ: In ordinary speech, saying one cannot bear speaking with someone means it is burdensome, not literally impossible. TABRISI: The verse disproves the Mujabbira's allowance of obligations beyond ability: capacity lies within human power, beyond which effort is exhausted. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: The verse means God does not impose what a person cannot do, since that would be impossible, like requiring a paralytic to run or a blind person to see. IBNJAWZI-ZAD: The prayer later in the verse asks not to be burdened with what cannot be borne; if impossible obligations could never be imposed, that request would be pointless. RAZI-FULL reporting المعتزلة: The Muʿtazila cite this verse and 22:78, 4:28, and the promise of ease to argue that God does not impose what a person cannot do. RAZI-FULL reporting أصحابنا: They argue that a genuinely impossible act cannot be requested in supplication, like combining opposites or making the eternal originated; abandoning this rule in particular cases needs specific evidence. RAZI-FULL: A difficult burden can be carried or imposed, while what is beyond capacity cannot be carried at all; therefore the verse uses “impose” for the impossible and both verbs for hardship. BAYDAWI-FULL: This supports the nonoccurrence of an impossible duty, but does not prove that such a duty is impossible in principle; compare 2:185. BURSEVI reporting التيسير: The request means not to impose duties that are difficult to sustain continually; it does not ask for the literally impossible, which cannot occur. {"id": "2:286/q07", "question": "Why do كَسَبَتْ and ٱكْتَسَبَتْ differ?", "turns_on": "The alternatives differ over the wording, scope, or evidence cited in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "2:286/q07/p1", "position": "The augmented form for evil suggests effort or intensity.", "reasons": "QURTUBI-FULL reporting ابن عطية: Ibn Atiyya says good deeds come without strain along God’s path, while evil requires forcefully breaching His prohibition; the two verb forms suit that distinction. NASAFI-FULL: Good is called kasb and evil iktisab because the iftiʿāl form suggests recoil: the soul recoils from evil and exerts itself for good. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting السجاوندي: Al-Sajāwandī explains the intensified form by saying evil clings to its doer, while good may be shared through guidance and intercession; iftiʿāl also suggests contraction, as the soul contracts into evil. BURHAN: The statement that every soul acquires only against itself concerns evil alone, by the occasion of revelation or by construing the verb as committing sin; the parallel verse states both good and evil, hence its contrast in verb forms. BIQAI-FULL reporting الحرالي: Al-Ḥarālī says the unaugmented verb denotes the least degree of earning, so even intending a good deed without doing it earns a good deed. ALUSI-FULL: The unaugmented kasabat suits good, which does not involve the same striving; iktasabat signals the soul's inclination to work at evil. MAWARDI-FULL: The forms may differ only in wording while sharing a meaning, or kasabat may be reserved for good and iktasabat for evil. IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting قوم: One view distinguishes kasabat for a single occurrence and iktasabat for repeated acts over time. IBNJAWZI-ZAD reporting آخرون: Another view treats kasabat and iktasabat as two forms with the same meaning, as in 86:17. QURTUBI-FULL: The verb kasaba is repeated with different morphology to suit the pleasing pattern of the speech. ABUHAYYAN-FULL reporting ابن عطية: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the verb is repeated in different forms simply to vary the style, as in the pairing of مهل and أمهل. BURHAN: The extra syllable in اكتسبت suits the burden and effort of sin, contrasting with the lighter form كسبت for good. BIQAI-FULL: The augmented iftiʿāl form for evil signals effortful engagement: sin is recorded only with firm resolve, and a person who intends evil but does not act is not charged.
